idea.title: Follow along: what a dental oral cancer check covers
idea.hook: Your dentist checks these at every visit. Can you find them first?
idea.brief: Each shot prompts the viewer to look at one area in their own mouth, lips, gums, tongue, cheeks, palate, throat, in the same order a dentist would. After the self-check, a single title card notes that most early oral cancers are found during routine dental visits, and that people who skip that care tend to reach diagnosis at later stages when outcomes are worse. The reel closes with a prompt to take a free risk screener at oralcheck.org/learn/prevention.

entries.hook: Your dentist checks these at every visit. Can you find them first?
entries.caption:
A routine dental visit includes a short check of the lips, inside of the cheeks, sides of the tongue, and roof of the mouth. Most early oral cancers are found this way. People who skip that care tend to reach diagnosis at later stages, when outcomes are worse. This reel walks through the same four areas in the order a dentist checks them. If something looks or feels off, bring it to a provider. Take the free risk screener at oralcheck.org/learn/prevention.

idea.title: Banned at the Brewers’ ballpark since 2016
idea.hook: One thing has been banned at the Brewers’ ballpark since 2016.
idea.brief: World Series week (Brewers v Rays). Milwaukee's 2016 smokeless tobacco ban at city sports venues (WUWM), MLB's ban for new players nine days later (SI), why (NCI: causes oral cancer; ACS: leukoplakia often where it is held between teeth and gums), and what to check. Hand-built by Claude at Ian's request, 26 Oct; Ian chose team colours and the logo.

entries.hook: One thing has been banned at the Brewers’ ballpark since 2016.
entries.caption:
Since November 2016, smokeless tobacco has been banned at every sports venue in Milwaukee, the Brewers’ ballpark included. The Common Council voted 14 to 1, and the Brewers backed it. Nine days later, Major League Baseball banned it for every new player.

The reason is in the mouth. Chewing tobacco causes oral cancer. Gray-white patches called leukoplakia are often found where it sits between the teeth and gums, and they can become cancer.

If you dip, pull your lower lip down and look at that spot. A patch still there after two weeks is worth showing a dentist. Check your own risk, free and private, at oralcheck.org.

Game 4 is tonight. Go Brewers.

Not affiliated with or endorsed by the Milwaukee Brewers or Major League Baseball.

idea.title: HPV overtook tobacco as the top throat cancer cause
idea.hook: Tobacco is not the leading cause of throat cancer anymore.
idea.brief: The correction lands first: tobacco has been overtaken by HPV as the primary driver of oropharyngeal cancers, meaning the tonsils, base of tongue and back of the throat. The supporting figure follows: HPV-positive cases rose 225% from 1988 to 2004 while HPV-negative ones fell by half (Chaturvedi 2011). A final line holds the nuance in place, noting that tobacco remains the biggest driver of cancers in the mouth itself, so this shift is specific to the throat. Picture: Ian's HPV and tobacco photos side by side, each with its figure. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

entries.hook: Tobacco is not the leading cause of throat cancer anymore.
entries.caption:
HPV has overtaken tobacco as the primary driver of oropharyngeal cancers, meaning the tonsils, the base of the tongue, and the back of the throat. Population-level incidence of HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancers rose 225% from 1988 to 2004, while HPV-negative ones fell by half.

That shift is specific to the throat. Tobacco is still the biggest driver of cancers in the mouth itself, so the risk picture depends on exactly where you're looking.

Knowing what's driving risk now is the first step toward catching anything early. Learn more and take the free screener at oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

Sources:
Chaturvedi et al., J Clin Oncol 2011. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21969503/

idea.title: A biopsy turns a white patch into an answer
idea.hook: You notice a white patch. You wait. It is still there.
idea.brief: Slide 1 states the myth: if a clinician looks at it and says nothing urgent, it must be fine. Slide 2 takes it apart: no one, not a clinician and not a photograph, can tell a harmless patch from a dangerous one by eye alone. Slide 3 names what actually gives an answer: a small tissue sample taken under local anaesthetic and examined under a microscope, a short appointment, not a procedure to dread. Final slide: oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

entries.hook: A clinician said nothing urgent. That is not the same as fine.
entries.caption:
You notice a white patch. You wait. It is still there.

A clinician glances at it and says nothing urgent. That feels reassuring, and it is easy to understand why. But "nothing urgent" and "nothing to investigate" are not the same thing.

No clinician, and no photograph, can look at a white or red patch in your mouth and know what it is. The cells beneath the surface do not announce themselves visually. A harmless patch and a changing one can look identical. That is not a gap in training. It is a limit of what any eye can detect.

The only thing that gives you an actual answer is a biopsy: a small tissue sample, taken under local anaesthetic, examined under a microscope. It is a short appointment. Most people find it far less involved than the word "biopsy" suggests. And it is the one step that turns a months-long worry into something you can act on.

If you have a white or red patch that has been there for more than two weeks, that is reason enough to ask for one.

Learn more about what these patches mean and when to push for further investigation at oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

idea.title: Halloween: what looks scary in your mouth, and what quietly matters
idea.hook: Some things in your mouth look frightening and are not. One looks like nothing and is.
idea.brief: A Halloween post that is a little spooky: the slides render in a night theme (moon, bats, a cobweb), and the words can carry a light spooky touch (things that look frightening, the one that should haunt you, what lurks quietly), but the facts stay calm and exact. No gore, no fear-mongering, no exclamation marks, never 'we'. Slide 1: the alarming-looking things that are usually harmless, from the facts (geographic tongue, thrush that wipes away, a burn from hot food, lacy lichen planus on both cheeks, a callus from a bitten cheek). Slide 2 compares the two sides: looks scary but usually harmless, against looks like nothing but worth a check (a painless patch or sore that is new and still there after two weeks). Slide 3: early oral cancer often does not hurt, so no pain is not reassurance. Close on the two-week rule and oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

entries.hook: Some things look frightening. One looks like nothing.
entries.caption:
Some things in your mouth look frightening and are not. One looks like nothing and is.

Geographic tongue moves around the tongue over weeks and is harmless. Oral thrush wipes clean away. A burn from hot food or drink heals on its own. Lacy white lines on both cheeks at the same time are almost always lichen planus. A callus from a cheek you bite settles once the cause is gone.

None of those are the thing to watch for.

What actually lurks quietly is a patch or sore that is new, doesn't hurt, and is still there two weeks later. No pain. No obvious cause. Just still there.

Early oral cancer often doesn't hurt at all, which is exactly why the two-week rule exists. Painless is not the same as harmless.

If something in your mouth has been there for more than two weeks and you can't explain it, that's the moment to act. Learn what to look for at oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

idea.title: Six HPV throat cancer symptoms worth knowing
idea.hook: Six symptoms can point toward HPV-related throat cancer.
idea.brief: The hook names the count, then the caption lists all six in plain language: a sore throat that hasn't resolved in two weeks, a painless neck lump, food that feels like it's catching, one-sided ear pain without an ear infection, hoarseness lasting more than two weeks, and unexplained weight loss. A closing sentence notes that none of these is proof of anything, but any one persisting beyond two weeks is worth getting checked. Photo shows a person touching their neck or throat, candid and unposed. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

entries.hook: Six symptoms can point toward HPV-related throat cancer.
entries.caption:
Six symptoms can point toward HPV-related throat cancer.

A sore throat that hasn't resolved in two weeks. A painless lump in the neck. Food that feels like it's catching when you swallow. Ear pain on one side with no ear infection to explain it. Hoarseness lasting more than two weeks. Unexplained weight loss.

None of these is proof of anything on its own, but any one of them persisting beyond two weeks is worth getting checked. Learn more at oralcheck.org/learn/hpv

idea.title: The two-week rule for a sore in your mouth
idea.hook: Most mouth sores heal on their own within two weeks.
idea.brief: Slide 1 describes what a canker sore looks like: round or oval, white or yellow center, red rim, painful, appearing only inside the mouth. Slide 2 marks the window: 7 to 14 days is the normal healing time. Slide 3 covers what does not follow that pattern: a lesion that is often painless early, has irregular or raised or hard edges, may bleed when touched, and is still there on day 15. Final slide: day 15 is when the sore gets checked, at oralcheck.org/learn/canker-sore-vs-oral-cancer.

entries.hook: Most mouth sores heal on their own within two weeks.
entries.caption:
Most mouth sores heal on their own, and that is the part worth holding onto.

A canker sore is round or oval, has a white or yellow center with a red rim, and is usually painful from the start. It shows up inside the mouth and clears within seven to fourteen days without any treatment.

A lesion that doesn't follow that pattern looks and behaves differently. It's often painless early on, which is part of why it gets ignored. The edges may be irregular, raised, or hard rather than smooth. It may bleed when touched. And on day 15, it's still there.

That's the signal. Not the size, not the pain level. The fact that it hasn't healed.

If you have a sore that's still present after two weeks, oralcheck.org/learn/canker-sore-vs-oral-cancer walks through what to look for and when to act.

idea.title: Painless patches: the warning sign that feels like nothing
idea.hook: No pain, no problem. That logic does not apply here.
idea.brief: Open on the contrast: pain is what most people wait for, but early oral cancer frequently does not hurt. Cut to a close shot of the inner cheek, then the tongue, showing where red and white patches appear and noting both can be completely painless. Close with the two-week rule: if a patch is still there after two weeks, that absence of pain is not reassurance. Check it at oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

entries.hook: No pain, no problem. That logic does not apply here.
entries.caption:
Pain is what people wait for. Early oral cancer often does not cause any. Red and white patches on the inside of the cheek or the sides of the tongue can be completely painless, which is exactly why waiting for discomfort is unreliable. The two-week rule exists for this reason: if a patch hasn't gone after two weeks, the absence of pain isn't reassurance. Learn what to look for at oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

idea.title: The two-week rule, place by place
idea.hook: Anything new in your mouth gets two weeks. Here is where to look.
idea.brief: A calm 3D walk through the places to check, each paired with the same question: is it still there after two weeks? Start on the sides of the tongue, then the floor of the mouth, then the gums. Name what counts: a sore, a patch, a lump or a colour change. Most things heal within two weeks; what has not deserves a look from a dentist or doctor, and it often does not hurt. Close on oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

entries.hook: Anything new in your mouth gets two weeks. Here is where to look.
entries.caption:
Canker sores and minor cuts heal within two weeks. Oral cancer lesions don't. The difference often isn't pain; it's persistence. Run through the sides of your tongue, the floor of your mouth, and your gums. A sore, a patch, a lump, or a colour change that's still there after two weeks deserves a look from a dentist or doctor. idea.title: The floor of your mouth is the hardest spot to self-check
idea.hook: Lift your tongue to the roof of your mouth right now.
idea.brief: The instruction opens the post and doubles as the self-exam itself. The caption explains what the viewer is looking at: the U-shaped tissue under the tongue, one of the highest-risk sites in the mouth, and one that can hide a small tumor for months before causing any discomfort. The closing line reinforces that the only way to see it is this exact move, which is why most people have never looked. Photo shows a person using a small mirror to examine the inside of their mouth. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

entries.hook: Lift your tongue to the roof of your mouth right now.
entries.caption: That U-shaped tissue you can see underneath is called the floor of the mouth, and it's one of the highest-risk sites for oral cancer. A small tumor there can grow for months without causing any pain or obvious change, which means most people never notice it until it's well advanced. The only way to see this area is exactly what you just did, and the fact that it takes a deliberate move is part of why these tumors get missed. Take thirty seconds, use a small mirror, and look at every part of that tissue from one side to the other. If you spot anything unusual, a pale patch, a dark spot, or a sore that hasn't healed in two weeks, it's worth getting it checked. Learn what to look for at oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

idea.title: Your lower lip gets more sun than you think
idea.hook: Sunscreen on your face, nothing on your lips.
idea.brief: A surprising-fact carousel, not a how-to (Ian: people already know how to check their tongue; swap for something more interesting, like a did-you-know). Open on the gap most people leave: sunscreen on the face, nothing on the lips. Then the facts: chronic sun exposure is a leading risk factor for cancer of the lower lip (not for cancers inside the mouth); the lower lip is the most common lip site; people who work outdoors are at higher risk. Close on the fix: SPF lip balm and a wide-brimmed hat offer meaningful protection. Calm, no scare tactics.

entries.hook: Sunscreen on your face, nothing on your lips.
entries.caption:
Sunscreen on your face, nothing on your lips. Chronic sun exposure is a leading risk factor for lower lip cancer specifically. It does not raise risk for cancers inside the mouth the same way. The lower lip is also the most common lip site for these cancers, and people who spend years working outdoors carry a higher risk than most.

Two habits make a real difference: SPF lip balm and a wide-brimmed hat. Neither requires a prescription or a clinic visit.

If you want to understand your own risk picture more fully, the free screener at oralcheck.org takes about two minutes.

entries.hook: 2.6 times. That's how much more often men are diagnosed.
entries.caption:
2.6 times. That's how much more often men are diagnosed with oral cancer than women, according to SEER age-adjusted incidence data.

That gap isn't concentrated only in older age groups. HPV-related throat cancer tends to show up in men between 40 and 60, which means the risk arrives earlier than most people expect.

Knowing where the risk sits is the first step toward doing something about it. Learn more at oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

idea.hook: Have you felt a lump in your neck that just will not go away?

entries.hook: Have you felt a lump in your neck that just will not go away?
entries.caption:
A painless lump in the neck is one of the more commonly missed early signs of HPV-related throat cancer. It shows up on the sides of the neck, just below the jaw, because it involves the lymph nodes in that area. The threshold worth knowing: a swollen node that stays for more than two weeks without an obvious infection is worth a conversation with your doctor. idea.title: Quitting tobacco still cuts oral cancer risk, even now
idea.hook: Tomorrow is the Great American Smokeout.
idea.brief: Myth slide: 'The damage is already done, so quitting now won't change much.' Fact slides: Tobacco is the single biggest modifiable risk factor for oral cancer, and risk drops measurably within a few years of stopping. Long-term ex-users approach the risk level of people who never used tobacco at all. Final slide lands on the plain truth: it is never too late for quitting to count. Close with the prompt to take the free risk screener at oralcheck.org/learn/prevention.

entries.hook: Quitting now still changes your risk. Here's the proof.
entries.caption:
Tomorrow is the Great American Smokeout, and one of the most persistent things people tell themselves about tobacco is that it is already too late to bother stopping.

It is not.

Tobacco is the single biggest modifiable risk factor for oral cancer, which means it is the one thing on that list you can actually do something about. And the research is clear: risk drops measurably within a few years of quitting. Stay quit long enough, and your risk can approach that of someone who never used tobacco at all.

There is no expiration date on that benefit. No point at which the body stops responding to the change.

If you use tobacco now, or you have in the past, understanding your current risk level is a reasonable place to start. The free screener at oralcheck.org/learn/prevention takes a few minutes and gives you a clearer picture of where you stand.

idea.title: When Gum Disease Is Not Gum Disease

Land on the one clue that separates them: a tooth that has come loose without any dental explanation, which is worth reporting to a clinician rather than waiting out. entries.hook: Gum disease and gum cancer can look nearly identical.
entries.caption:
Gum disease and gum cancer share a lot of the same signs: redness, swelling, tissue that looks or feels off. The one clue that sets them apart is a tooth that comes loose without any dental reason behind it. That's worth mentioning to a clinician rather than waiting to see if it resolves. idea.title: Five common mouth findings that are not oral cancer
idea.hook: Five things in your mouth that look worrying but probably aren't.
idea.brief: The hook sets up relief rather than alarm, then the caption walks through each: frictional keratosis from a bitten cheek or ill-fitting denture, oral thrush that wipes away, lichen planus with its fine lacy lines on both cheeks, a burn from hot food that heals within days, and geographic tongue with its shifting pale-bordered patches. The closing line shifts the frame: the list isn't a reason to ignore changes, it's context for the one rule that matters, which is that anything new still present after two weeks deserves a look. Photo shows a close-up of lips or an open mouth in soft natural light. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

entries.hook: Five things in your mouth that look worrying but probably aren't.
entries.caption:
A white patch or a sore spot can send you straight to a spiral of worst-case thinking. Before that happens, it helps to know what the common lookalikes actually are.

1. Frictional keratosis. A callus that forms where a cheek gets bitten repeatedly, or where a sharp tooth or ill-fitting denture rubs. It tends to settle once the source of irritation is gone.

2. Oral thrush. A yeast infection that wipes away.

3. Lichen planus. Fine white lacy lines, usually on both cheeks at once.

4. A burn from hot food or drink. It looks alarming for a few days, then heals.

5. Geographic tongue. Smooth red areas with pale borders that appear to shift position on the tongue over days or weeks. Harmless.

None of this is a reason to stop paying attention. The rule that holds regardless of what you find is straightforward: anything new that's still there after two weeks deserves a proper look. Learn more about white and red patches at oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

entries.hook: Before the leftovers, two minutes and a mirror.
entries.caption:
Before the second round of pie, take two minutes with a mirror.

The people gathered around your table this week are often the ones best placed to notice a change in your face or neck. But a monthly self-exam means you can spot something first.

Start at your lips and work inward: cheeks, gums, tongue (top, sides, and underneath), the floor of your mouth, the roof of your mouth, your throat, and then both sides of your neck. You're looking for anything new: a patch, a sore, a lump, or a change in colour.

The two-week rule is worth knowing. Early oral cancer often doesn't hurt, so pain isn't a reliable guide. If something new is still there after fourteen days, that's the moment to call a dentist or doctor and have it looked at.

Share this with someone at the table who might not have heard of the two-week rule. And for a step-by-step illustrated guide, oralcheck.org/learn/self-exam is there whenever you're ready.

idea.title: Low-cost oral care options when you have no dentist
idea.hook: When did you last have someone look inside your mouth?
idea.brief: Slide 1 names the reader directly: this post is for anyone without a dentist, without insurance, or without money for a private appointment. Slide 2 lays out three options side by side: HRSA-funded community health centers that charge on a sliding scale, dental schools that offer lower-cost care, and free clinics that exist in many areas. Final slide: oralcheck.org/find-care searches all of them by location.

entries.hook: When did you last have someone look inside your mouth?
entries.caption:
No dentist. No insurance. No budget for a private appointment. That combination stops a lot of people from ever getting their mouth looked at, and it doesn't have to.

Community health centers charge on a sliding scale based on what you earn. Dental schools offer care at lower cost, supervised by licensed faculty. Free clinics exist in more places than most people expect. None of them require full-price insurance to walk through the door.

oralcheck.org/find-care searches all three by your location. If cost or coverage has been the reason you haven't gone, this is the place to start.

idea.title: Gardasil 9 approved through age 45, most effective earlier
idea.hook: The vaccine works best before exposure. It's still available after.
idea.brief: The contrast between ideal timing and real-world eligibility is the spine of the post. The caption explains that Gardasil 9 protects against HPV-16 and HPV-18, the strains behind most HPV-related cancers, and that it's FDA-approved for ages 9 through 45. Adults who weren't vaccinated earlier may still benefit, and the caption notes that a doctor can advise on individual circumstances. One plain closing sentence clarifies what the vaccine cannot do: it can't treat an existing infection. Photo shows a young adult in a clinical setting, receiving a routine injection, candid rather than staged. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

entries.hook: The vaccine works best before exposure. It's still available after.
entries.caption: Gardasil 9 targets HPV-16 and HPV-18, the strains responsible for most HPV-related cancers, and it's FDA-approved for anyone between 9 and 45. The recommended window is early, ideally before any exposure, which is why preteens are the primary target. That said, adults who weren't vaccinated earlier may still get meaningful protection, and a doctor can help weigh whether it makes sense for your situation. One thing it can't do is treat an infection that's already there. If you're unsure where you stand, start at oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

idea.title: Two white patches that look alike but are not the same
idea.hook: Two patches in your mouth look almost identical.
idea.brief: Slide 1 describes oral thrush: a yeast infection whose white coating wipes away, often leaving a red sore area underneath. Slide 2 describes leukoplakia: a patch that stays put when you try to rub it away. Slide 3 holds the line that matters for both: neither can be confirmed by eye, and any patch that is still there after two weeks gets checked. Final slide: oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

entries.hook: Two white patches. One is fine. One isn't.
entries.caption:
Two white patches can sit in the same mouth and look almost identical. One wipes away. One doesn't.

Oral thrush is a yeast infection. The coating comes off with gentle pressure and often leaves a raw, red area underneath. Leukoplakia is different: a thickened patch the tissue produces that stays put no matter how much you rub.

The catch is that neither can be confirmed by eye. A clinician can't call it from a photo, and you can't call it from a mirror. What you can do is pay attention to time. A patch that's still there after two weeks is one that gets examined.

If you've noticed something and you're not sure what to make of it, a free risk screen is a reasonable first step. Learn more at oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

Have you ever noticed a patch in your mouth and talked yourself out of getting it checked?

idea.title: Leukoplakia: the white patch that cannot be scraped off
idea.hook: A white patch you can rub off is one thing. One you cannot is another.
idea.brief: Open on the contrast between a food residue or thrush that clears with rubbing and a leukoplakia that stays fixed to the tissue. Show the most common sites: the inner cheek, the tongue, and the floor of the mouth. Note that leukoplakia is usually painless, which is why it goes unnoticed for months, and that while most are benign, a share become malignant if left untreated. If a white patch will not come off and has no clear explanation, check it at oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

entries.hook: A white patch you can rub off is one thing. One you cannot is another.
entries.caption:
A white patch that wipes away is usually harmless. One that stays fixed to the tissue, with no clear cause, is worth taking seriously. Leukoplakia is painless most of the time, which is exactly why it goes unnoticed for so long. The inner cheek, the tongue, and the floor of the mouth are the places it tends to show up. If a patch won't come off, learn what to look for at oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

3D anatomy: Z-Anatomy (CC BY-SA 4.0), from BodyParts3D, DBCLS

idea.title: Betel quid raises oral cancer risk with or without tobacco
idea.hook: Tobacco-free doesn't mean risk-free. Not with betel quid.
idea.brief: The contrast opens the post by challenging an assumption, then the caption grounds it in IARC's classification: betel quid, whether it contains tobacco or not, is a Group 1 carcinogen for oral cancer. That includes areca nut, paan and gutka. The closing line explains why the OralCheck screener asks about it specifically: the risk is independent of tobacco, so leaving it off a standard risk checklist would miss a meaningful exposure. Photo shows betel leaves and areca nut on a surface, or a market stall with paan ingredients. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/screener.

entries.hook: Tobacco-free doesn't mean risk-free. Not with betel quid.
entries.caption: Betel quid without tobacco is still classified as a Group 1 carcinogen for oral cancer by the WHO's cancer agency, IARC. That classification covers areca nut, paan and gutka. The risk isn't borrowed from tobacco. It stands on its own. Most standard risk checklists don't ask about betel quid, which means a real exposure goes unrecorded. The OralCheck screener asks about it specifically because missing it would leave a meaningful gap in the picture. Take the free screener at oralcheck.org/screener.

idea.title: Mixed red-and-white speckled patches carry the highest risk
idea.hook: A patch that is partly red, partly white carries more risk than either alone.
idea.brief: Open on the contrast between a uniformly white patch and a speckled mix of red and white, naming the latter as the higher-risk type. Tour four sites in the mouth one at a time: the inner cheek (label: buccal mucosa), the tongue's lateral edge (label: lateral tongue), the floor of the mouth (label: floor of mouth), and the soft palate (label: soft palate), with one spoken line at each noting this is where speckled patches are found. Close on the defining rule: if it does not rub or scrape off, it needs a professional look. More at oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

entries.hook: A patch that is partly red, partly white carries more risk than either alone.
entries.caption:
Most mouth sores heal in a week or two. A speckled red-and-white patch that won't rub away is a different thing, and it tends to appear in four specific spots: the inner cheek, the side of the tongue, the floor of the mouth, and the soft palate.

That one rule is worth remembering. If it does not scrape off, it needs a professional eye on it, not more waiting.

Learn what to look for and take a free risk screener at oralcheck.org/learn/white-and-red-patches.

idea.title: Survival rates for oral cancer by stage at detection
idea.hook: Oral cancer caught while still localized has an 89% five-year survival rate.
idea.brief: Slide 1 puts 89% at full size with one line of context: that is the five-year relative survival rate when oral cancer is found while it is still localized, according to SEER data. Slide 2 shows what changes as it spreads: about 70% once it reaches nearby tissue, about 36% once it has spread to distant sites. Slide 3 names what moves those numbers in the right direction: regular screening and not waiting on a sore or patch that does not heal, starting at oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

entries.hook: Oral cancer caught early has an 89% survival rate.
entries.caption:
Oral cancer caught while still localized has an 89% five-year survival rate. Once it has spread to distant sites, that figure falls to 36%. The gap between those two numbers is not luck. It is timing.

Only about 26% of oral cancer cases are found while still localized, which means most are caught after the odds have already shifted. Regular screening and acting on a sore or patch that does not heal in two weeks are the two things most likely to change that.

Learn what the research shows and take a free risk screener at oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

idea.title: HPV exposure is common and most infections clear
idea.hook: Have you ever thought about whether you've been exposed to HPV?
idea.brief: A single calm sentence over a candid photo of two adults in conversation: 'Most sexually active adults have been exposed to HPV at some point, and the vast majority of infections clear on their own.' A second line notes that certain strains, particularly HPV-16, can drive DNA changes that lead to cancer in some people, which is why knowing your risk matters. Caption closes by directing viewers to oralcheck.org to take the free screener.

entries.hook: Have you ever thought about whether you've been exposed to HPV?
entries.caption:
Most sexually active adults have been exposed to HPV at some point, and the vast majority of infections clear on their own without ever causing symptoms. Certain strains, particularly HPV-16, can drive DNA changes that lead to cancer in some people. That's why knowing your risk matters, even if you feel completely fine. Take the free oral cancer risk screener at oralcheck.org.

idea.title: Reference card: oral cancer warning signs beyond colour
idea.hook: Run your finger along the inside of one cheek.
idea.brief: The card is laid out in plain document style, built to be saved. Three entries, each with a short label and a one-line description: irregular, raised, or hardened edges on a sore or patch; a sore that bleeds easily when touched; and a new lump or thickening in the cheek, tongue, gum, or floor of the mouth, often firm, like a pea under the skin. Footer line: any of these lasting more than two weeks gets checked at oralcheck.org/learn/signs.

entries.hook: Run your finger along the inside of one cheek.
entries.caption:
Run a finger along the inside of your cheek right now. You're not looking for colour alone. The signs worth catching early are often textural: an edge on a sore that feels raised or hardened, a spot that bleeds when you brush against it, or a small firm lump sitting just under the surface of the cheek, tongue, gum, or floor of the mouth.

Most sores heal on their own within a week or two. The ones that don't are the ones that need attention. Two weeks is the line. If something is still there at that point, it's worth getting checked.

The full list of signs to watch for is at oralcheck.org/learn/signs. Save this card if it's useful to you.

idea.title: Tobacco plus alcohol together multiply oral cancer risk
idea.hook: Do you smoke and drink? The combined risk is not what you might expect.
idea.brief: Open with the question framing the viewer's own habits, then move through three sites where tobacco and alcohol damage the same tissue together: the floor of the mouth (label: floor of mouth), the lateral tongue (label: lateral tongue), and the soft palate (label: soft palate). At each stop, one spoken line explains that both substances act on the same lining, and that alcohol may help tobacco carcinogens enter the cells. Close on the figure from the Hashibe 2009 pooled analysis: heavy smokers who also drink heavily face about 15 times the risk of people who do neither, and cutting back on either one brings that risk down. Run a free screen at oralcheck.org/learn/risk-factors.

idea.title: HPV throat cancer at the base of tongue and tonsils
idea.hook: You open wide, look in the mirror, and see nothing unusual.
idea.brief: Start in that moment: the viewer has done what seems like a reasonable self-check and found nothing. Then explain that HPV-related cancers tend to start at the base of the tongue and the tonsils, an area called the oropharynx that sits too far back to see in a bathroom mirror. Because there is often no visible lesion and the site is hard to examine, these cancers are frequently caught later than cancers that appear on the lips or front of the tongue. Close with the practical step: a structured screener can flag the risk factors that a mirror cannot. Start at oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

idea.title: Median age at diagnosis is 65, but age alone rules nothing out
idea.hook: 65 is the median age at diagnosis. It isn't the only age to watch.
idea.brief: The figure and its limit occupy the same breath. The caption acknowledges that 65 is the SEER median, then immediately complicates it: HPV-related throat cancers are appearing more often in middle-aged adults, and age alone is no longer a reliable reason to dismiss a symptom. The post doesn't reframe 65 as irrelevant; it makes the case that a number is a midpoint, not a boundary. Photo shows a person in their forties or early fifties at a routine medical appointment, seated and attentive. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

idea.title: Red patch in your mouth: what it means
idea.hook: Pull your cheek aside and look at the inner lining.
idea.brief: Slide 1 opens with the physical instruction and names the reader directly: if you spot a flat red patch that has been there two weeks or more and does not hurt, this post is for you. Slide 2 introduces erythroplakia by plain description only, noting it is far less common than a white patch and easy to dismiss precisely because it is painless and undramatic. Slide 3 delivers the key fact: studies estimate 50% or more of red patches are already cancerous or precancerous at biopsy, making it the single most concerning thing you can find on your own. Final slide closes with a clear, calm instruction: if you found something that fits, do not wait for your next cleaning to mention it. Run a full self-check now at oralcheck.org.

idea.title: 60,480 new oral cancer cases expected in the US this year
idea.hook: How many Americans will be diagnosed with oral cancer this year?
idea.brief: The question hangs for a beat before the caption answers it: an estimated 60,480 in 2026, according to SEER. The second sentence gives the other number without dressing it up: about 13,150 are expected to die of it. The closing line connects scale to action, noting that a free screener takes about two minutes and is the most concrete thing someone can do today. Photo shows a realistic crowd scene, a busy public space like a train station or market, to give the numbers a sense of physical scale without being graphic. Caption closes with oralcheck.org/learn/facts.

idea.title: HPV-related oral cancer in men with no tobacco history
idea.hook: You have never smoked. You assume that lowers your risk.
idea.brief: Slide 1 sits with that assumption: for a long time, oral cancer was understood as a disease tied to tobacco, which made it easy to feel unaffected without that history. Slide 2 names the group most commonly diagnosed with HPV-related throat cancer: men between 40 and 60, most of them with no history of tobacco use. Slide 3 closes without alarm, just a prompt: knowing the full picture of risk is what makes early checking useful, at oralcheck.org/learn/hpv.

idea.title: Two-minute oral self-exam you can do right now
idea.hook: Get a mirror and find a light source.
idea.brief: Each shot covers one area in the order a clinician would move through it: face and neck, lips, cheeks, gums, tongue top, tongue sides, tongue underside, floor of the mouth, roof of the mouth, then throat. On screen text for each shot names the area and tells the viewer exactly what to look for: anything new, a patch, a sore, a lump, or a colour change. The final frame holds on a plain slate: once a month, every month, oralcheck.org/learn/self-exam.

entries.hook: Get a mirror and find a light source.
entries.caption:
This takes about two minutes, once a month, with a mirror and a good light. Move through the inside of your cheek, your tongue, the roof of your mouth, and under your jaw, looking for anything that's new: a patch, a sore, a lump, or a colour change. If something stays beyond two weeks, get it checked by a clinician. Learn the full exam at oralcheck.org/learn/self-exam.
